title: Freddie Keppard, early jazz bands and the Chicago split
summary: Keppard did not record; he recalls the Original Creole Orchestra, Chicago clubs and the Oliver band break-up.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: No, no. Well he might have not wanted to. You know a lot of guys, Freddie Kepa didn't want to record. A lot of guys didn't want to record. You see a lot of guys didn't want to record.
Did you ever talk to Freddie Kepa about that?

I never did do any talking to Freddie at all. I can remember just how high Freddie, or one of them things. Freddie didn't want to record because he said he'd steal his stuff. See he didn't want to record. Last I saw Freddie became sick. Freddie was a big man around 250. And he came down the last time I saw him, it looked like he was about 160 or something like that. I do believe, well I don't know, it could have been most anything was wrong, but he died, he should have died. He'd come into the club room and get him half a pint of his moon, you know, and go on a corner by himself. He'd drink after a while and get up and leave. And they didn't have much to say until the fellas. Talking about Freddie, do you remember his brother? No. I didn't know his brother played in that original band that left here, supposed to have been 1911, but I didn't know him.
You never heard him play? No, as I know of.

A lot of guys I heard play I didn't know who they were, you know, as a kid I didn't know who they were. He was up in Chicago. He just sounded good and I ran behind him, huh? He was up in Chicago too. Well he might have, evidently. They made a hit in New York and everywhere they went. That was some different kind of music you know. And the people just went for it. Just like Chicago they ate it up. Big crowds wherever they played. Three or four bands playing in the places, the Lord of the Lord, the Tony Jacksons was playing at the Panama on the first floor, you know. And upstairs was the Luxors, the New Orleans band, across the street, the New Orleans band. Over 35th, it's two or three. It's one down, the two hours down to Peekin, 26th Street, and he's got a power ball around and he's playing over the man of the president playing in the Royal Garden. There's Clarence Williams at the music store there, 31st Street, you know. Oh there was a lot going on in New Orleans, New Orleans. And the guys began to think about those guys. They said, these guys came in and got over the job. But then they began to have them hassles among themselves. You see, after Dutre and Dodd found out that Joe had substituted New Orleans and Atkins, well that caused hard feelings. The band busted up soon. And Johnny Dodd was taking the man into this place over there. They had them tables, no tablecloths or on there. Kelly's tables, yeah. Kelly's tables, he and Dominic did Dutre. And Louie, he left and went to New York. And Lil, eventually had a band owned at the Dreamland. And so they just split up. Imagine them fellas came back to New Orleans. I'm going to have to run this after six now. I think they hit eight a couple. . . .
